course.title: Probability & Statistics II
course.description: A second pass through probability and statistical inference — from the probability rules and the binomial distribution to the normal curve, the Central Limit Theorem, confidence intervals, and hypothesis testing. Extends Introductory Statistics, with structure and topics adapted from OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e (CC BY 4.0).

questions.prompt: The probability of any event must be a number between…
questions.explanation: Probabilities run from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain) — see 'Probability rules'.

questions.prompt: Two events are independent when…
options: one event happening does not change the other's probability
questions.explanation: Independence means no influence on each other's probability — see 'Probability rules'.

questions.prompt: A binomial experiment requires…
options: a fixed number of independent trials, each with two outcomes
a probability that changes every trial
questions.explanation: Fixed n, two outcomes, constant p, independent trials — see 'The binomial distribution'.

questions.prompt: The standard normal distribution has…
questions.explanation: The standard normal is centered at 0 with spread 1 — see 'The normal distribution and z-scores'.

questions.prompt: A z-score tells you…
options: how many standard deviations a value sits from the mean
questions.explanation: z measures distance from the mean in standard-deviation units — see 'The normal distribution and z-scores'.

questions.prompt: The Central Limit Theorem says the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately…
options: normal for a large enough sample
questions.explanation: For large n the mean's distribution is roughly normal, whatever the population's shape — see 'Sampling distributions and the CLT'.

questions.prompt: A 95% confidence interval means…
options: 95% of the data lie inside the interval
the method captures the true parameter about 95% of the time
there is a 95% chance this one sample is correct
questions.explanation: Confidence is about the long-run success rate of the method — see 'Confidence intervals to hypothesis testing'.

questions.prompt: A small p-value (say 0.01) provides…
options: strong evidence against the null hypothesis
proof that the null hypothesis is true
evidence the sample was too small
questions.explanation: A small p-value means the data would be surprising if the null were true — see 'Confidence intervals to hypothesis testing'.

lessons.title: The rules of probability
lessons.grammar_note: 'And' points to the multiplication rule; 'or' points to the addition rule. Read the connector first.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: State and apply the addition, multiplication, and conditional-probability rules, and reason about a Bayes-style update. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what is the smallest and largest value a probability can take?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A probability is a number from 0 to 1 measuring how likely an event is. Two rules do most of the work. The addition rule handles 'or': P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B), where you subtract the overlap so it is not counted twice. The multiplication rule handles 'and': P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B given A). When A and B are independent, P(B given A) is just P(B), so P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). Worked example: draw one card from a 52-card deck. P(king or heart) = 4/52 + 13/52 - 1/52 = 16/52, which is about 0.31 — the lone king of hearts is the overlap you subtract.

sections.heading: Conditional probability and a Bayes update
sections.text: Conditional probability asks: given that B happened, how likely is A? The formula is P(A given B) = P(A and B) / P(B). Worked example: roll one fair die. P(rolling a 2, given the roll is even) = P(2 and even) / P(even) = (1/6) / (3/6) = 1/3. Bayes intuition flips a conditional around. Suppose a disease affects 1% of people, a test catches it 90% of the time in sick people, but also flags 10% of healthy people. If you test positive, how worried should you be? P(positive) = 0.90 x 0.01 + 0.10 x 0.99 = 0.009 + 0.099 = 0.108, so P(sick given positive) = 0.009 / 0.108, about 0.083 — only around 8%. Because the disease is rare, most positives are false alarms.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue marbles. (1) P(drawing red) on one draw? (2) Drawing two without replacement, P(both red)? (3) Rolling one fair die, P(greater than 4)? (4) If P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, and P(A and B) = 0.2, find P(A or B). (5) If A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.6, find P(A and B). Answers: (1) 3/5 = 0.6; (2) 3/5 x 2/4 = 6/20 = 0.3; (3) 2/6 = 1/3; (4) 0.5 + 0.4 - 0.2 = 0.7; (5) 0.3 x 0.6 = 0.18.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: adding P(A) + P(B) for 'or' without subtracting the overlap. Mistake: treating P(A given B) as the same as P(B given A) — the disease example shows they differ wildly. Mistake: assuming events are independent when one truly affects the other (drawing without replacement). Exit: (a) Write the addition rule. (b) Write the formula for P(A given B). Answers: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B); P(A given B) = P(A and B) / P(B).

lessons.title: The binomial distribution
lessons.grammar_note: Binomial checklist: fixed n, two outcomes, constant p, independent trials. Miss one and it is not binomial.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Recognize a binomial setting and compute a binomial probability, mean, and standard deviation. Warm-up: name one experiment with exactly two outcomes on each trial.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A binomial experiment runs a fixed number n of independent trials, each a success (probability p) or failure (probability 1 - p). The chance of exactly k successes is P(X = k) = C(n, k) x p^k x (1 - p)^(n - k), where C(n, k) counts the ways to place the k successes among n trials. The distribution's mean is np and its standard deviation is the square root of np(1 - p). Worked example: flip a fair coin 5 times (n = 5, p = 0.5). P(exactly 3 heads) = C(5, 3) x 0.5^3 x 0.5^2 = 10 x 0.125 x 0.25 = 0.3125. The mean number of heads is np = 2.5, and the standard deviation is the square root of 1.25, about 1.12.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Quality check: a machine makes parts that are defective 20% of the time (p = 0.2). In a box of 10 independent parts, P(none defective) = P(X = 0) = 0.8^10, which is about 0.107 — roughly an 11% chance of a clean box. The expected number of defects is np = 10 x 0.2 = 2. Guessing on a quiz: 4 multiple-choice questions with 4 options each means p = 0.25 for a lucky guess. P(getting 0 right by guessing) = 0.75^4, about 0.316, so a blind guesser walks away empty-handed nearly a third of the time.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) n = 4, p = 0.5: find P(exactly 2 successes). (2) n = 3, p = 0.5: find P(all 3 successes). (3) Find the mean of a binomial with n = 20 and p = 0.1. (4) Find the standard deviation of a binomial with n = 100 and p = 0.5. (5) A 4-question guessing quiz (p = 0.25): find P(0 correct). Answers: (1) C(4, 2) x 0.5^2 x 0.5^2 = 6 x 0.0625 = 0.375; (2) 0.5^3 = 0.125; (3) np = 2; (4) square root of 100 x 0.5 x 0.5 = square root of 25 = 5; (5) 0.75^4 = about 0.316.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: forgetting the C(n, k) count and multiplying only the probabilities. Mistake: using n instead of np for the mean. Mistake: calling trials binomial when p changes between them (drawing without replacement). Exit: (a) Write the mean of a binomial. (b) In 5 fair-coin flips, what is P(exactly 3 heads)? Answers: mean = np; 0.3125.

lessons.title: The normal distribution and z-scores
lessons.grammar_note: z = (value - mean) / standard deviation. Positive z is above the mean, negative is below.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Convert a raw value to a z-score and use the empirical rule to estimate proportions. Warm-up: what are the mean and standard deviation of the standard normal distribution?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The normal distribution is the symmetric bell curve; a z-score rewrites any value as its distance from the mean in standard-deviation units: z = (x - mean) / standard deviation. The empirical rule (68-95-99.7) says that in a normal distribution about 68% of values fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within 2, and about 99.7% within 3. Worked example: IQ scores have mean 100 and standard deviation 15. A score of 115 has z = (115 - 100) / 15 = 1.0, so it sits one standard deviation above the mean, with about 84% of people scoring below it (50% below the mean plus 34% between the mean and z = 1).

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Adult heights with mean 170 cm and standard deviation 10 cm: the interval from 160 cm to 180 cm is exactly mean plus or minus 1 standard deviation, so about 68% of people fall inside it. A height above 190 cm is beyond 2 standard deviations above the mean; since 95% lie within 2 standard deviations, 5% lie outside, split evenly, so about 2.5% are taller than 190 cm. A test score with mean 500 and standard deviation 100: a 700 has z = (700 - 500) / 100 = 2.0, placing it two standard deviations above the mean, near the 97.5th percentile.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: A dataset has mean 50 and standard deviation 5. (1) Find the z-score of x = 60. (2) Find the z-score of x = 45. (3) By the empirical rule, what percent lies within 2 standard deviations? (4) For mean 500 and standard deviation 100, find the z-score of x = 700. (5) A value has z = 0; if the mean is 80, what is x? Answers: (1) (60 - 50) / 5 = 2; (2) (45 - 50) / 5 = -1; (3) about 95%; (4) (700 - 500) / 100 = 2; (5) x = 80, since z = 0 sits exactly at the mean.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: forgetting the sign — a value below the mean has a negative z. Mistake: dividing by the variance instead of the standard deviation. Mistake: treating the empirical rule as exact rather than approximate. Exit: (a) Write the z-score formula. (b) What percent of a normal distribution lies within 1 standard deviation of the mean? Answers: z = (x - mean) / standard deviation; about 68%.

questions.prompt: A fair die is rolled once. P(rolling a 5 or a 6) is…
questions.explanation: Two favorable outcomes out of six: 2/6 = 1/3.

questions.prompt: Two independent events have probabilities 0.4 and 0.5. P(both occur) is…
questions.explanation: For independent events, multiply: 0.4 x 0.5 = 0.2.

questions.prompt: In 5 flips of a fair coin, P(exactly 3 heads) is…
The mean of a binomial distribution with n = 50 and p = 0.4 is…
A value two standard deviations above the mean has a z-score of…
questions.explanation: z counts standard deviations from the mean, so z = 2.

questions.prompt: By the empirical rule, about what percent of a normal distribution lies within 1 standard deviation of the mean?
questions.explanation: The 68-95-99.7 rule: about 68% within 1 standard deviation.

lessons.title: Sampling distributions and the Central Limit Theorem
lessons.grammar_note: Standard error of the mean = standard deviation / square root of n. Bigger samples, smaller error.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Compute the standard error of the mean and explain what the Central Limit Theorem guarantees. Warm-up: if you took many samples and averaged each, would those averages vary more or less than individual values?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Take many samples of size n and record each sample's mean; those means form a sampling distribution. Its spread, the standard error, is the population standard deviation divided by the square root of n: standard error = standard deviation / square root of n. The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) says that for a large enough n, this sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal and centered on the true population mean, no matter what shape the population has. Worked example: a population has mean 70 and standard deviation 12. For samples of size 36, the standard error = 12 / square root of 36 = 12 / 6 = 2, so sample means cluster around 70 with a spread of 2 — far tighter than individual values.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A population with standard deviation 20 sampled at n = 100 gives a standard error of 20 / square root of 100 = 20 / 10 = 2. Because the sampling distribution is roughly normal, you can z-score a sample mean: with population mean 70 and standard error 2, a sample mean of 73 has z = (73 - 70) / 2 = 1.5, so it lands one and a half standard errors above the expected value — mildly high but not shocking. Notice the pattern: quadrupling the sample size (from 25 to 100) only halves the standard error, because the square root of 4 is 2.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) Population standard deviation 10, n = 25: find the standard error. (2) Standard deviation 15, n = 9: find the standard error. (3) As n grows, does the standard error rise or fall? (4) Standard deviation 20, n = 400: find the standard error. (5) A population is strongly skewed; for n = 200, what is the approximate shape of the sampling distribution of the mean? Answers: (1) 10 / 5 = 2; (2) 15 / 3 = 5; (3) it falls; (4) 20 / 20 = 1; (5) approximately normal, by the CLT.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: dividing by n instead of the square root of n. Mistake: thinking the CLT makes the population itself normal — it is the distribution of the sample mean that becomes normal. Mistake: expecting big samples to increase the spread of the mean; they shrink it. Exit: (a) Write the standard error of the mean. (b) What does the CLT say happens to the sample mean's distribution as n grows? Answers: standard deviation / square root of n; it becomes approximately normal.

lessons.title: From confidence intervals to hypothesis testing
lessons.grammar_note: Reject the null when the p-value is below alpha (often 0.05); otherwise fail to reject. You never 'accept' the null.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Build a confidence interval and run a one-sample t-test, then read a p-value correctly. Warm-up: from the CLT, what quantity describes the spread of sample means?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for a population mean: sample mean plus or minus (critical value) x (standard error). For a 95% interval the critical value is about 1.96. Worked example: a sample of n = 100 has mean 50 and standard deviation 10, so the standard error = 10 / square root of 100 = 1, and the 95% interval is 50 plus or minus 1.96 x 1 = 50 plus or minus 1.96, that is (48.04, 51.96). Hypothesis testing turns the same machinery into a decision. Set a null hypothesis (H0, 'no effect', e.g. mean = 100) and an alternative (Ha). Compute a t-statistic: t = (sample mean - null mean) / (standard deviation / square root of n). The p-value is the probability of a t at least this extreme if H0 were true; reject H0 when the p-value falls below alpha.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Test one: H0 says mean = 100. A sample of n = 25 has mean 104 and standard deviation 15, so the standard error = 15 / 5 = 3 and t = (104 - 100) / 3 = 1.33. With 24 degrees of freedom, a two-tailed p-value is about 0.20 — larger than 0.05, so we fail to reject H0; the 4-point gap is within ordinary sampling noise. Test two: H0 says mean = 50. A sample of n = 25 has mean 56 and standard deviation 10, so the standard error = 10 / 5 = 2 and t = (56 - 50) / 2 = 3.0. With 24 degrees of freedom, the two-tailed p-value is about 0.006 — well below 0.05, so we reject H0; a gap that large would be very surprising under the null.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) For a 95% confidence interval, what critical value do you use? (2) A sample mean is 20 with standard error 2; give the 95% interval using 1.96. (3) If the p-value is 0.03 and alpha is 0.05, what is the decision? (4) If the p-value is 0.20 and alpha is 0.05, what is the decision? (5) With sample mean 52, null mean 50, standard deviation 8, and n = 16, compute t. Answers: (1) about 1.96; (2) 20 plus or minus 1.96 x 2 = 20 plus or minus 3.92, that is (16.08, 23.92); (3) reject H0; (4) fail to reject H0; (5) standard error = 8 / 4 = 2, so t = (52 - 50) / 2 = 1.0.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading a 95% interval as '95% of the data'; it is about the method capturing the parameter 95% of the time. Mistake: calling a large p-value proof that H0 is true — it only means the data are consistent with it. Mistake: dividing by n rather than the square root of n in the standard error. Exit: (a) When do you reject the null hypothesis? (b) What does a p-value measure? Answers: when the p-value is below alpha; the probability of data at least this extreme if the null were true.

items.translation: a number from 0 to 1 measuring how likely an event is
items.example: The probability of a fair coin landing heads is 0.5.

items.translation: the probability of one event given that another has occurred, P(A given B) = P(A and B) / P(B)
items.example: Given that a die roll is even, the conditional probability it is a 2 is 1/3.

items.translation: the distribution of the number of successes in a fixed number of independent two-outcome trials
items.example: The count of heads in 5 coin flips follows a binomial distribution.

items.translation: how many standard deviations a value lies from the mean: (value - mean) / standard deviation
items.example: An IQ of 115 has a z-score of 1.0 when the mean is 100 and the standard deviation is 15.

items.translation: the rule that the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal for a large sample
items.example: Thanks to the Central Limit Theorem, sample means are bell-shaped even when the population is skewed.

items.translation: the probability of data at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis were true
items.example: A p-value of 0.006 is strong evidence against the null hypothesis.

questions.prompt: The standard error of the mean equals…
options: the standard deviation divided by n
the standard deviation divided by the square root of n
the square root of the standard deviation
questions.explanation: Standard error = standard deviation / square root of n.

questions.prompt: A population has standard deviation 10 and you sample n = 25. The standard error is…
questions.explanation: 10 / square root of 25 = 10 / 5 = 2.

questions.prompt: The critical value for a 95% confidence interval is about…
questions.explanation: About 1.96 standard errors capture the middle 95%.

questions.prompt: A 95% confidence interval means the method captures the true parameter…
questions.explanation: Confidence describes the long-run success rate of the procedure.

questions.prompt: You reject the null hypothesis when the p-value is…
questions.explanation: A p-value below alpha signals evidence against the null.

questions.prompt: A p-value of 0.002 indicates…
options: strong evidence against the null hypothesis
strong evidence for the null hypothesis
only that the sample was large
questions.explanation: Such extreme data would be very unlikely if the null were true.

lessons.title: Applied project: design a hypothesis test

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Plan a one-sample hypothesis test for an everyday claim you could investigate (for example, 'the average wait at this coffee shop is 4 minutes' or 'students at my school sleep 7 hours a night'). You will not collect the full dataset — you will design the test rigorously and reason about the outcome.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) State the null and alternative hypotheses in plain language and in symbols (for example, H0: mean = 4 versus Ha: mean is not equal to 4). 2) Describe how you would draw an unbiased sample and roughly how large it would be, and name the standard error you would compute. 3) Write the t-statistic formula you would use and explain how you would obtain a p-value from it. 4) State your decision rule (reject H0 if the p-value is below your chosen alpha, otherwise fail to reject) and explain what each outcome would mean in the real-world terms of your claim.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: Correct if: your hypotheses are complementary and testable; your sampling plan is unbiased and its size is justified; your test statistic is the sample mean minus the null mean, divided by the standard error; and your conclusion language says 'reject' or 'fail to reject' rather than 'prove'. If all four hold, you have reasoned like a statistician — you turned a vague claim into a decision backed by probability.
